source.version: RETRIEVAL MISMATCH. The file on disk is not the c493 record (Mir Djawadi and Fahr, AEA RCT Registry AEARCTR-0016306, 2025). It is Haase and Hanel, 'Artificial muses', downloaded from https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.12003 (retrieval.json source 'arxiv_title'). The PDF itself shows no version number or date. The text says data were collected in early February 2023 and that GPT-4 was released on 14 March 2023 (p. 4, p. 12).
source.title_on_document: Artificial muses: Generative Artificial Intelligence Chatbots Have Risen to Human-Level Creativity

supplement.where: Referred to as 'supplemental materials'; no URL given. Data and R code at https://osf.io/9fctd/?view_only=6c8f02c6972b49319c12f87cfb3f76db (p. 4).
supplement.holds: Table S1 (intraclass correlations of the human raters), Figure S1 (AI-rated originality, human vs GAI), Figure S2 (AI-rated comparison of the GAIs), and all fluency results (p. 4, p. 5, p. 8).

paper_design_summary: The document on file (Haase and Hanel, arXiv 2303.12003) is not the c493 trial registration. In it, 100 Prolific participants completed five Alternative Uses Test prompts without any AI, and five GAI chatbots (later GPT-4 as well) answered the same prompts. Six human raters and an AUT-trained language model scored originality, blind to the source, and the paper compares human-generated with chatbot-generated responses; no person received AI help.

studies.label: Alternative Uses Test: 100 humans vs six GAI chatbots

assignment.what_was_assigned: No assignment to AI. Only the order of the five AUT prompts was randomized for human participants.
assignment.quote: In the present study, we compared the creativity of GAI chatbots with humans: We applied the Alternative Uses Test (AUT) to 100 human participants and five GAI.

arms.name: Humans
arms.description: Prolific participants who wrote alternative uses for five objects, three minutes per object, without AI.

arms.name: GAI chatbots
arms.description: Alpa.ai, Copy.ai, ChatGPT (GPT-3), AI21 Studio, YouChat; GPT-4 added in follow-up analyses rated only by the AI. Prompt 'What can you do with [prompt]?', with 'What else?' up to three times.

participants.exclusions: None stated for participants. No-answers and unrelated answers were excluded at the response level (p. 12).
participants.who: Native English speakers from the USA with full- or part-time work, mean age 41.00 (SD 12.25), 50 women and 50 men; paid US$9 per hour; mean completion 17 minutes.
participants.quote: In total, 100 participants completed our study (Mage = 41.00, SD = 12.25, 50 women, 50 men), who were recruited through Prolific Academic.

ai_tool.name_model: Alpa.ai, Copy.ai, ChatGPT (GPT-3), AI21 Studio (Jurassic-1), YouChat; GPT-4 in follow-up analyses
ai_tool.how_used: The chatbots produced AUT responses themselves; no human used them.

task.description: Alternative Uses Test for five objects: pants, ball, tire, fork, toothbrush.
task.duration: Three minutes per object for humans; average completion time 17 minutes.

outcomes.name: Originality rated by six human raters (CAT, 1-5 scale)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Six human raters, blind to source, following the Consensual Assessment Technique on a 1-5 originality scale; ICC .85 to .94 (Table S1). Responses averaged per creator and prompt. Linear mixed model with random intercepts and slopes for prompt; per-prompt between-subjects t-tests in Table 1.

outcomes.name: Originality rated by an AUT-trained language model
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Large language model trained on prior human AUT ratings (Organisciak et al.); correlation with mean human rating rs = .78 to .94. Same mixed model and per-prompt t-tests.

contrasts.reported: Humans more creative than GPT-4: 2 (pants), 29 (ball), 0 (tire), 3 (fork), 13 (tooth); on average 9.4 humans across prompts. AI-rated only.

outcomes.name: Fluency (number of ideas)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Sum of ideas per participant or chatbot, by the AI and the six raters. Chatbots were prompted up to three extra times.

contrasts.reported: GAI chatbots came up with 2-3 times more ideas than humans; full results in the supplemental materials.

company_involvement.description: Funded in part by the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research (16DII133).

eligibility.reason: The document on file is Haase and Hanel (arXiv 2303.12003), not the c493 record. It compares chatbot-generated AUT responses with responses from 100 humans who worked without AI; no person was assigned to AI assistance, so it is ai_vs_human context. The c493 record itself (Mir Djawadi and Fahr, AEARCTR-0016306) is a trial registration with no results on file and cannot be screened from this PDF.

one_line_finding: Five GAI chatbots matched 100 humans on AUT originality (human-rated mixed model B = -0.21, SE = 0.15, p = .218; AI-rated B = -0.18, SE = 0.13, p = .241; p. 4, Table 1 p. 5), and on average 9.4 humans beat GPT-4 (p. 7).
open_questions: Retrieval mismatch: retrieval.json for c493 points to arXiv 2303.12003 (Haase and Hanel, 'Artificial muses'), which shares only the generic title words with the c493 record (Mir Djawadi and Fahr, AEA RCT Registry AEARCTR-0016306). The registration entry needs its own retrieval or a status of 'registration only, no results'.
If Haase and Hanel is not already a separate candidate, it may belong in the ai_vs_human context list under its own cid.
The paper does not say which group is coded 1 in the mixed models, so the sign of B is not interpretable from the text.
notes: Filled for the document on file. The registration (planned 50-70 adults and 50-70 children per arm, matchstick task, per candidates.json) is not in this PDF, and nothing about it is recorded here. Human rater identity (lay or expert) is not stated; the acknowledgments name six people who rated responses (p. 1). Table 1 has five rows labeled Pants, Ball, Tire, Fork, Tooth.
